title: Flow Matching
interviewAnswer: Flow matching trains a model to predict a continuous velocity field that transports samples from a simple distribution such as noise toward the data distribution. Inference integrates that learned vector field over time.
why: Flow matching is increasingly important in modern generative modeling because it offers a direct vector-field view of transporting simple noise distributions into complex data distributions.
intuition: Instead of learning “what noise should I remove?”, imagine learning a velocity arrow at every intermediate point that tells the sample how to move from a simple source distribution toward real data.
deepDive: Choose a probability path connecting source noise x₀ to target data x₁. Sample an intermediate xₜ and train a network vθ(xₜ,t) to match the target velocity field. At inference, solve the ODE dx/dt=vθ(x,t) from source to data. Rectified-flow variants choose simple paths that can make trajectories easier to integrate.
math: For a simple straight interpolation xₜ=(1-t)x₀+t x₁, the target conditional velocity is x₁-x₀ (details vary by formulation/path).
code:
# Conceptual pseudocode
x0 = sample_noise()
x1 = sample_data()
t = uniform(0, 1)
xt = (1-t)*x0 + t*x1
target_v = x1 - x0
pred_v = model(xt, t, condition)
loss = mse(pred_v, target_v)
commonMistakes: Treating every flow-matching implementation as exactly the straight-line formula above; practical paths/objectives vary.
Saying flow matching and MMDiT are synonyms: one is a training/generative formulation, the other is an architecture family.
followUps: How is flow matching different from diffusion?
What ODE solver is used at inference?
How does conditioning enter the velocity network?
production: Inference speed depends on number of function evaluations and solver choice; deployment still needs benchmarking rather than assuming flow matching is always faster.
workedExample: For conditioned microstructure reconstruction, the velocity network can use bottleneck embeddings while transporting noise toward a sample consistent with those embeddings.

lab.goal: Implement a rectified-flow training target on toy points.
lab.buildIt:
import torch
x0=torch.randn(256,2); x1=torch.randn(256,2)+torch.tensor([3.,0.])
t=torch.rand(256,1); xt=(1-t)*x0+t*x1; target=x1-x0
model=torch.nn.Sequential(torch.nn.Linear(3,64),torch.nn.Tanh(),torch.nn.Linear(64,2))
opt=torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(),1e-3)
for _ in range(300):
    pred=model(torch.cat([xt,t],1)); loss=((pred-target)**2).mean()
    opt.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); opt.step()
print(loss.item())
lab.useIt:
# Euler integration at inference: x <- x + dt * v_theta(x,t)
x=torch.randn(32,2); dt=.05
for i in range(20):
    tcur=torch.full((32,1),i/20)
    with torch.no_grad(): x += dt*model(torch.cat([x,tcur],1))
